Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural clinics in Eritrea primarily use paper-based recording for patient data at point of care, with aggregate data later entered into DHIS2 for reporting. DHIS2 connects 342 facilities (2018), including rural ones, via offline decentralized entry, but pre-DHIS2 relied on pen-and-paper, and no evidence confirms direct digital patient registration in most rural clinics. Recent tracker program aims at patient-level data, but implementation unclear; computers procured for districts (2020), digital platforms planned for hospitals, not clinics. Barriers: limited internet/power, suggesting reliance on aggregation not PoS digital. National HIS ambition exceeds rural PoS reality, typical of low-resource settings. Score 2 as digital limited to aggregate reporting/pilots.

revision_notes: Fetched all three originally cited sources; none describes digital data capture occurring at the rural clinic itself. The 2024 DHIS2 conference abstract describes decentralised data entry occurring at zone/sub-zone level with centralised analysis, not facility-level digital capture, and the WHO UHC partnership monitoring entry confirms DHIS2 roll-out to 'lower levels' is still a supported activity rather than a completed state. The 2018 Shabait piece confirms the pre-DHIS2 baseline was pen-and-paper. Per the metadata guidance, only facility-level capture counts (higher-level aggregation digitisation is excluded), so the evidence supports 'Entirely paper' (code 1) as originally scored; confirmed, not changed.
revised_comments: Rural clinics in Eritrea record patient data on paper at the point of care. Aggregate data is subsequently entered into the DHIS2 platform, but this entry occurs at zone or sub-zone level rather than through digital capture at the clinic itself. The Ministry of Health has introduced a DHIS2 tracker module intended to support patient-level data in future, and WHO's UHC partnership monitoring records continuing support for extending DHIS2 to lower levels of the health system, but no evidence indicates this has yet translated into routine digital data capture within rural clinics. Limited rural electricity and connectivity continue to constrain facility-level digitisation.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Extensive searches across web, academic papers, US State Dept HR reports, UK guidance, UNODC, Shabait (gov news), OSAC security report yield no evidence of digital case management, incident reporting, or records systems in Eritrean police, including rural stations. Recent digital initiatives (customs ASYCUDA, library digitization, police computer training) exist but not for police records. Eritrea's centralized, militarized, low-resource police structure (district stations, manual investigations per Criminal Procedure Code) and lack of mentions in intl reports imply entirely paper-based recording at rural facilities, consistent with most African countries without specific digitalization evidence. No rural-specific contradiction found; score 1 per instructions favoring paper if no digital evidence.

A further search found a 2026 report of computer-maintenance and networking training for serving police officers, which evidences general IT skills training but not deployment of any digital records or case-management system at station level. No authoritative source describes digitisation of record-keeping at rural (or any) Eritrean police stations, so the absence-of-evidence basis for 'Entirely paper' stands; confirmed, not changed.
revised_comments: No official source documents a digital case-management, incident-reporting, or records system in Eritrean police stations, including rural stations. Recent Ministry of Information reporting describes new recruits and serving officers receiving general computer-maintenance and networking training, but this reflects basic IT skills training rather than deployment of an electronic records system. Eritrea's police structure remains centralised, militarised and resource-constrained, and available evidence points to record-keeping at rural stations remaining entirely paper-based.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Eritrea lack dedicated civil status officers, resulting in entirely paper-based or non-existent birth registration processes. Births are declared via manual forms from local administrative areas (e.g., district committees), requiring witnesses and later court approval if delayed, then processed at urban municipal offices like Asmara. No evidence of electronic CRVS, DHIS2, or digital point-of-service recording in rural areas; urban areas have some network systems for population registers, but rural facilities do not. Key barriers include resource shortages, lack of policy enforcement, optional registration, low awareness, and no infrastructure for offices in rural zones (80%+ population). National policy under Transitional Civil Code exists but unimplemented rurally; 2025 UN metadata confirms no functional CRVS system countrywide, relying on old DHS surveys. Gap: Urban selective registration vs. rural absence; pilots absent.

revision_notes: Fetched the UN Statistics Division 2025 vital statistics metadata questionnaire, which explicitly states there is no functional and complete CRVS system in Eritrea, and the older (2002) Kampala workshop report describing rural areas as having no civil status officer at all. A January 2025 UN Committee on the Rights of the Child session record confirms the government is still working towards a 90%-by-2028 registration strategy rather than describing an operational digital rural registry. No source found describes any digital or electronic recording at rural registry offices. The evidence supports 'Entirely paper' (code 1); confirmed, not changed.
revised_comments: Eritrea has no functional, complete civil registration and vital statistics system, and rural areas lack civil status officers altogether, so births, deaths, and marriages there are recorded, if at all, through informal, manual declarations rather than at a dedicated registry office. The UN Statistics Division's 2025 vital statistics metadata questionnaire for Eritrea confirms there is no functional and complete CRVS system, with national vital statistics still derived from Demographic and Health Surveys (1995, 2002, 2010) rather than routine registration. The government has told the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (January 2025) that it is pursuing a strategy to reach 90% birth registration nationwide by 2028, indicating that rural civil registration capacity remains largely undeveloped and paper-based at present.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Eritrea rely on paper-based questionnaires and annual school censuses for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes, which are collected by Zoba education offices and sent to the Ministry of Education. Questionnaire 7 and 8 cover enrollment data from November each year, with 100% collection rate reported, but no mention of digital tools at school level; process implies manual filling and physical/digital transmission higher up. EMIS exists at national level since World Bank project (2003-2012), used for policy alongside GIS (not integrated), but school-level input remains paper-default per annual stats process. No evidence of routine digital recording (computers/tablets) at rural point-of-service; rural areas lack electricity/infrastructure for ICT, widening digital divide. Barriers: poor electricity/telecom in remote areas, inadequate ICT resources/maintenance, limited teacher training. National EMIS ambition contrasts with rural paper reality; data aggregated upward post-collection, fitting score 2 (predominant paper, digital for aggregate reporting).

A 2025 journal article on Eritrea's EMIS confirms its data-collection tools still date from a 1993 design, and 2024 Global Partnership for Education documents note that education data collection, management and storage require strengthening, corroborating that no digital capture occurs at the school facility itself. Per the metadata guidance that only facility-level capture counts, the evidence supports 'Entirely paper' (code 1), matching the value actually recorded; confirmed, not changed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Eritrea record enrolment, attendance and other administrative data on paper, which is compiled through standardised questionnaires submitted to Zoba (regional) education offices for entry into the Ministry of Education's national Education Management Information System. The Ministry's Basic Education Statistics 2023/24 report, published in December 2024, is produced through this annual paper-based census process. Academic research on Eritrea's EMIS notes that its data-collection tools still reflect a design dating from 1993, and Global Partnership for Education programme documents note that education data collection, management and storage require further strengthening. Limited rural electricity and telecommunications infrastructure continues to constrain any facility-level digital data capture, and no evidence indicates that rural schools themselves capture data digitally at the point of collection.
